title: GOP Gerrymandering is Erasing the South’s Black Votes
author: Jordan Liz
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/05/2024_United_States_presidential_election_in_Tennessee_under_2022_and_2026_congressional_districts.svg-680x344.png)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/05/15/gop-
gerrymandering-is-erasing-the-souths-black-votes/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/05/2024_United_States_presidential_election_in_Tennessee_under_2022_and_2026_congressional_districts.svg-680x344.png)

Photograph Source: Longestview -
[CC0](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/deed.en)

On May 8, the Republican-controlled legislature of
[Tennessee](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-election/tennessee-
republicans-pass-map-splitting-states-lone-majority-black-di-rcna343934)
passed new redistricting maps that divide Memphis’s 63 percent Black
population across three white-majority districts. This eliminates the state’s
sole Black-majority district.

Republicans in [Alabama](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/05/11/supreme-
court-allows-alabama-gop-to-erase-black-house-district-00915541),
[Louisiana](https://www.npr.org/2026/05/04/nx-s1-5807903/louisiana-lawmakers-
working-to-pass-map-that-could-eliminate-majority-black-districts),
[Mississippi](https://mississippitoday.org/2026/04/30/gerrymander-mississippi-
bennie-thompson/), and [Georgia](https://www.wabe.org/supreme-court-decision-
weakening-voting-rights-act-could-impact-future-political-maps-in-georgia/)
are similarly pushing redistricting maps that would decimate their majority-
Black districts.

These moves come on the heels of the Supreme Court’s controversial decision in
[ _Louisiana v. Callais_](https://www.commondreams.org/opinion/voting-rights-
act-backwards), which effectively killed Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act.
This was the latest in a decades-long effort by the [Supreme
Court](https://www.newyorker.com/news/the-lede/how-the-supreme-court-
demolished-the-voting-rights-act) to dismantle the law, reversing a signature
accomplishment of the Civil Rights Movement.

This systematic assault against the voting power of Black people is a
deliberate attempt to deny them political representation and silence their
voices.

Tennessee was admitted to the Union in 1796 but didn’t elect its first Black
congressperson, Representative [Harold Ford Sr.](https://steven-
knowlton.scholar.princeton.edu/sites/g/files/toruqf3746/files/steven.a.knowlton/files/a_democrat_for_all_the_people.pdf)from
Memphis, until 1974 — nearly 10 years after the passage of the Voting Rights
Act. That Memphis-based district is the very one now being dismantled.

Without the Voting Rights Act and the racial gerrymandering it was designed to
oppose, Ford may not have been elected.

Not because Black people only vote for candidates of color. It’s because
people, regardless of race, vote for those they believe understand their
problems and work to solve them. While we vote as individuals, the social,
political, and economic challenges we face are deeply interwoven with the
communities in which we live.

Black people are twice as likely as whites to face [food
insecurity](https://www.feedingamerica.org/hunger-in-america/black-
communities) and more likely to live in “[food
deserts](https://hub.jhu.edu/magazine/2014/spring/racial-food-deserts/).” This
reality is inextricably tied to the continuing influence of slavery and Jim
Crow.

This includes:
“[redlining](https://www.memphis.edu/law/about/ml14_rootsoffooddeserts.php),”
whereby mortgages and insurance were denied to people in minority-majority
neighborhoods; “[racial covenants](https://www.cnn.com/2020/02/15/us/racist-
deeds-covenants/index.html)” that prohibited people of color from renting,
buying, or occupying specific property; and
[segregation](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3956000/), which
concentrated poverty and restricted [social mobility](https://anderson-
review.ucla.edu/segregation-compounds-the-effects-of-poverty/).

These policies functioned for decades to keep Black communities underserved,
underinvested, and underdeveloped. They are the foundation of the [racial
wealth gap](https://www.brookings.edu/articles/black-wealth-is-increasing-but-
so-is-the-racial-wealth-gap/) that persists today. According to the [National
Community Reinvestment Coalition](https://ncrc.org/the-racial-wealth-
gap-1992-to-2022/), in 2022 the median white household held $284,310 — more
than six times the $44,100 held by the median Black household.

The racial wealth gap limits access to education, healthcare, and
opportunities as well as food. Larger grocery stores are less willing to open
stores in poor areas because they consider them less profitable. This is known
as “[supermarket redlining](https://theconversation.com/how-urban-planning-
and-housing-policy-helped-create-food-apartheid-in-us-cities-154433)”and
disproportionately impacts communities of color.

The fact of the matter is that, despite progress on these issues, people of
color continue to be impacted by [racism](https://www.pewresearch.org/race-
and-ethnicity/2024/06/15/racial-discrimination-shapes-how-black-americans-
view-their-progress-and-u-s-institutions-2/),
[colorism](https://jlhochschild.scholars.harvard.edu/publications/skin-color-
paradox-and-american-racial-order),
[Islamophobia](https://belonging.berkeley.edu/UPR4-consequences-of-
islamophobia), and
[xenophobia](https://humanrightsfirst.org/library/xenophobia-fact-sheet/) in
ways that white people are not. Politicians pretending these problems no
longer exist will only serve to widen racial inequalities.

Yet this is precisely what will occur if Republicans succeed in splitting the
Black vote across multiple white-majority districts.

Right now, the Democrats are largely focused on [counter-
gerrymandering](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/04/30/hakeem-jeffries-
voting-rights-act-gerrymandering-redistricting-2026-midterms-00900661) the
Republicans in other states. This may help them win seats, but it won’t help
the Black communities across the South that are being disenfranchised.

These political games must end. President [John Adams](https://press-
pubs.uchicago.edu/founders/documents/v1ch4s5.html) once wrote that the House
of Representatives “should be in miniature, an exact portrait of the people at
large. It should think, feel, reason, and act like them.”

Gerrymandering, however, inverts this equation. Instead of the House
reflecting the people, it reflects the will of the politicians who carve up
districts to gain political power. It is a government designed by the
politicians for the politicians.

We must put an end to racist  _and_ partisan gerrymandering. We must restore
the Voting Rights Act. And ultimately, we must ensure that Black communities
have the political representation they’ve earned via their [blood, sweat, and
tears](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/may/09/activists-supreme-
court-voting-rights-act).

Anything less is a betrayal of their struggle as well as the ideals of
America’s Founders.
